connector: Today you build your portfolio: three pieces of your own writing, one from each part of the year, and what each one shows. Put them side by side and you can see how you grew.

a.raw: marilla she demanded presently do you think that i shall ever have a bosom friend in avonlea
a.fixed: “Marilla,” she demanded presently, “do you think that I shall ever have a bosom friend in Avonlea?”
a.why: Anne’s real words (Ch. 8): the tag splits one sentence, so do stays lowercase; the question mark goes inside the last quotation mark.

b.raw: my best piece is my comparison paragraph because it uses evidence from two books
b.fixed: My best piece is my comparison paragraph because it uses evidence from two books.
b.why: Capital M to start; no comma needed before because at the end; a period ends it.

notes.wgrd: Reflect on how your reading habits have grown: who you were as a reader in August, who you are now, and the proof.
vocab: To change your writing to make the ideas better.
To check writing for mistakes in capitals, usage, punctuation and spelling.
A collection of your best work.
To think back on something and what it taught you.
notes.wordParts: Every base from the year: port, tract, struct, spect, ject, script, rupt, duct, form, press, tain, lev, plus prefixes like pre-, re-, trans-, inter-.
notes.grammar: Spiral review: capitals, commas, quotation marks, complete sentences. Read your sentence out loud and check each mark has a job.
notes.spelling: Spiral review: drop the silent e, change y to i, double the last consonant when the beat is on the last syllable, and spell each word part the same way every time.

transcripts.welcome: Hello again, it’s Opti. Today you build your portfolio. Today’s question: what can you do now that you couldn’t do in September?
transcripts.read: Find three pieces of your writing: one from the fall, one from the middle of the year, one from this spring. Pick the ones that show a skill, not the longest ones. Then put them side by side. What changed?
transcripts.spelling: One last spelling check. Read your piece out loud and touch each long word. Find the part you know. Check the ending. If a word looks strange, it probably is. Fix it now, and your best piece stays your best.
